summary: CNBC reports on how Amazon third-party sellers view the FTC's 172-page antitrust lawsuit accusing Amazon of using an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy box penalties to inflate prices. Some sellers on Seller Central cheered the suit as "long overdue," while others like Scott Needham and Scott Moller say the FTC picked issues that don't hurt them or that Amazon services like FBA actually help. Sellers such as Fred Ruckel and Molson Hart describe pricing-policy and fee problems, and Amazon's David Zapolsky defends the company's practices.
one_line: Amazon sellers give mixed reactions to the FTC's antitrust suit, with some calling it overdue and others doubting it would improve the marketplace.
key_facts: On Oct. 27, 2021, Fred Ruckel received an automated Amazon email saying his Ripple Rug cat toy was ineligible for the buy box because it was priced lower elsewhere.
Chewy dropped the Ripple Rug price to $39.99 versus $43 on Amazon, but the Chewy price was $48.54 after shipping and taxes; Ruckel asked Chewy to raise the price.

The FTC's 172-page lawsuit accuses Amazon of wielding monopoly power to squeeze merchants and thwart rivals, citing an "anti-discounting strategy" and a "massive web-crawling apparatus that constantly tracks online prices."
The FTC alleges that losing the buy box is an "existential threat" to sellers and that Amazon's tactics create an "artificial price floor everywhere."
The FTC has not yet outlined specific remedies, which in antitrust cases are often determined only after a court finds the defendant liable.
Amazon general counsel David Zapolsky said sellers set their own prices and that the lawsuit could force Amazon to stop highlighting low prices, "a perverse result."
On Amazon's Seller Central forum, several users cheered the FTC; one wrote "It's long overdue," while another called Amazon's message to sellers "BS verbiage."
Scott Needham, who sells on Amazon and runs a product-finder tool, said he was "surprised by some of the points that the FTC selected" and that many sellers "love FBA."
Needham said he would have supported the case more before the pandemic, noting competition from Shopify, Walmart and Temu has grown since 2019.
Scott Moller, who sells grilling accessories as Grill Sergeant, says FBA shipping costs him $7.49 per package versus about $12 shipping it himself.
Moller disputed the FTC's claim that ads clutter search results, saying ads let sellers target exactly the consumers they want.
Molson Hart of Viahart says Amazon accounts for about 90% of his business and he testified before a House committee in 2019 about seller fees and pricing.
In September 2022, Hart endured "24 anxious hours" when a third-party seller listed his Brain Flakes toy for less on Target than on Amazon.
